newsitem.title: MEXICO: Colombia sees Mexico, Venezuela trade pact revival.
newsitem.headline: Colombia sees Mexico, Venezuela trade pact revival.

text.p: Colombian Foreign Minister Maria Emma Mejia, winding up a two-day visit to Mexico, hailed as the main fruit of her trip Tuesday the revival of a trade pact between Colombia, Venezuela and Mexico.

The so-called Group of Three (G-3) free trade pact faced a stern test shortly after it was inked in 1994 when two of its signatories -- Mexico and Venezuela -- plunged into economic crisis and sharply devalued their currencies.

Mejia told Reuters in an interview that presidents of the G-3 nations now planned a special meeting to review and revitalize the accord on the sidelines of the next Ibero-American summit, which is to be held in Santiago in November.

"At times it looked like (the G-3) was stumbling," Mejia told Reuters in an interview. "But now with this commitment of the presidents which will be re-ratified in two months time in the Santiago summit, we are going to give it a (new) dimension."

Colombia was a big loser from the pact last year because its trade gap with Mexico widened to $362 million -- a gap Mejia said was Bogota's worst with any country -- but she insisted that President Ernesto Samper's administration remained committed to the G-3.
"It's better we have it than that we don't," Mejia said. "What we have to do is use it aggressively."

Mejia said Colombia's main hope for boosting exports to Mexico was through sales of coal. The country has a huge open pit steam coal mine close to the Caribbean coast, most of whose output is exported.
Other prospects included publishing, an area where Colombia is strong, and textiles, she added.

Colombian businessmen complained loudly at a breakfast meeting held earlier about the difficulties of exporting to Mexico. High on their list of gripes was the strong Colombian peso, which has revalued sharply in real terms over the past four years.
Mexico's ambassador to Colombia Oliver Farres told them that the trade deficit was to a certain degree compensated by the high level of Mexican investment in Colombia -- now more than $1.2 billion.
Two more large investments were likely by the year-end, he added, without elaborating.

Other problems raised by the businessmen included the difficulty of getting visas for Mexico in Bogota, thefts from shipments between the two countries, high freight costs, infrequent air service and alleged bad treatment at the hands of Mexican immigration officials.

Mejia said goverment efforts to devalue the peso were hindered by the fact that Colombia's central bank is independent, but added that she hoped exporter pressure would be sufficient to force the bank to change course.
The strong peso was good insofar as it indicated economic stability but was also "strangling in good measure Colombian exporters," she said.
